batchName: Early Republic: Final Conquest of Italy (290-264 BCE) - Easy Batch 2
chapterName: Early Republic: Final Conquest of Italy (290-264 BCE)

questions.question: How did Rome control most of the Greek cities of Magna Graecia after Pyrrhus left?
options: By handing them over to Carthage
By sending Roman governors to rule them
questions.explanation: Rather than rule them directly, Rome bound most of the Greek cities through treaties, giving it indirect control. Apart from garrisons, its grip stayed loose for decades.
questions.sourceQuote: Instead of ruling the Greek cities of Magna Graecia directly, it bound most of them through treaties.

questions.question: By the time he went to Sicily, what had Pyrrhus's ambitions grown into?
options: Conquering Egypt and the eastern kingdoms
Retaking his lost lands back in Greece
Dominating both southern Italy and Sicily
Capturing Rome and ruling all of Latium
questions.explanation: His goals had grown far beyond rescuing Tarentum. In the end, though, his Sicilian adventure brought him nothing lasting.
questions.sourceQuote: He aimed to dominate both southern Italy and Sicily.

questions.question: The Appian Way, Rome's great road, ran south from Rome toward which city?
questions.explanation: The Appian Way ran south toward Capua, carrying Roman armies and influence deep into the south. Rome also founded colonies of loyal citizens on conquered land.
questions.sourceQuote: It also built the Appian Way, a great road running south from Rome toward Capua, which carried armies and influence deep into the south.

questions.question: According to the Roman tradition preserved by Livy, what caused the last plebeian secession?
questions.explanation: The traditional account blamed debt, with angry crowds revolting when called up to fight the Lucanians. Modern historians doubt this version.
questions.sourceQuote: The Roman tradition, preserved in yearly chronicles and by the historian Livy, blamed debt.

questions.question: Where was Pyrrhus killed in 272 BC?
questions.explanation: Pyrrhus died fighting a different war at Argos in southern Greece. That same year, Tarentum fell to Rome.
questions.sourceQuote: That same year Pyrrhus himself was killed while fighting a different war at Argos, a city in southern Greece.

questions.question: What did Rome's system of colonies, citizenship and alliances turn Italy into?
options: A grain supplier for the Greek world
A single province under one governor
A vast reservoir of fighting men
A loose league of free kingdoms
questions.explanation: Rome's system produced a reservoir of soldiers larger than that of any other state of the time. Allies stayed independent in name but had to supply troops.
questions.sourceQuote: This system turned Italy into a vast reservoir of fighting men, larger than that of any other state of the time.

questions.question: Where did the Samnites, Rome's toughest rivals in central Italy, come from?
options: The Po Valley in the north
questions.explanation: The Samnites were a warlike coalition of tribes from the Apennine mountains. Rome fought them in three Samnite Wars between 343 and 290 BC.
questions.sourceQuote: Its toughest rivals had been the Samnites, a warlike coalition of tribes from the Apennine mountains.

questions.question: What does the phrase "Pyrrhic victory" mean?
options: A win gained by a surprise attack
A win so costly it is almost a defeat
A win won by hired foreign troops
A win achieved with no losses at all
questions.explanation: The phrase comes from Pyrrhus, whose victories over Rome cost his army terribly. He reportedly said, "Another such victory and we are lost!"
questions.sourceQuote: A "Pyrrhic victory" is a win that costs the victor so much that it is almost a defeat.

questions.question: Who was the next enemy to seriously challenge Rome's control of the Italian peninsula after Pyrrhus?
questions.explanation: Rome's hold on Italy was not seriously challenged again until Hannibal invaded at the end of the century. Its victory over Pyrrhus had hugely boosted its standing.
questions.sourceQuote: Its control of the Italian peninsula would not be seriously challenged again until Hannibal invaded at the end of the century.

questions.question: The Conflict of the Orders was a long struggle between which two groups in Roman society?
questions.explanation: For two centuries the hereditary patrician elite and the mass of ordinary plebeian citizens struggled over political rights. The Hortensian Law of 287 BC brought this conflict to a close.
questions.sourceQuote: For two centuries, Roman society had been split between the patricians, a small hereditary elite, and the plebeians, the mass of ordinary citizens.
